card.title: Measurement of specific heat capacity of solids and liquids

rows.label: Concept
rows.text: **Specific heat capacity** c is the heat per kilogram needed to raise temperature by one kelvin: $Q = mc\Delta T$ (J kg⁻¹K⁻¹); the whole-body version is heat capacity $C = mc$. Water's 4186 J kg⁻¹K⁻¹ is exceptionally high, making it nature's coolant.…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text: - Q = mcΔT; C = mc - m₁c₁(T₁−T) = (m_w c_w + m_c c_c)(T−T₂) - c_water = 4186 J kg⁻¹K⁻¹

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: **c vs C:** specific heat c (J kg⁻¹K⁻¹) is per kilogram; heat capacity C = mc (J/K) is for the whole body.  ·  **Water's huge c** makes it both a coolant and a climate stabiliser.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Dry the solid before weighing if it was in a boiling bath.  ·  A thermometer's heat capacity is usually neglected.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: Covers only: measurement of specific heat capacity of solids, liquids (within Quantity of Heat).  ·  Out of scope here: topics of neighbouring units in Physics — don't mix them.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Copy the worked example and hide the result until the last step.  ·  Name the unit of every term in the formula.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: "Balance: m₁c₁ΔT₁ = m₂c₂ΔT₂ — include the calorimeter term."

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: **Numerical (3m): A 0.2 kg iron block (c = 460) at 150 °C is dropped into 0.3 kg water at 20 °C. Find the final temperature (neglect calorimeter).** — 0.2×460×(150−T) = 0.3×4186×(T−20) → 92(150−T) = 1255.8(T−20) → 13800−92T = 1255.8T−25116 → T = 38916/1347.8 = 28.9 °C.

rows.text: Definition + one numerical is the standard 3m package (2023, 2024).

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: **The method of mixtures** turns the conservation-of-energy statement into a measurement instrument.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Q = mcΔT; c in J kg⁻¹K⁻¹; water 4186.  ·  Calorimetry: heat lost = heat gained (include the calorimeter!).

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Water's specific heat (4186) is the highest of common substances — coastal climates stay mild.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — How Much Heat for One Degree? Water needs 4186 J to raise one kilogram by one kelvin; copper needs barely a tenth of that. Specific heat capacity quantifies this appetite for heat — and the principle of calorimetry (heat lost = heat gained) turns mixtures into measurement instruments.  ·  ## 2. Fundamental Concepts (NEB 2020, 2023, 2024) ### 2.1 Definitions **Quantity of heat:** the energy transferred because of temperature difference; measured in joules. **Specific heat capacity (c):** the heat required to raise the temperature of **1 kg** of a substance by **1 K**: $$Q = mc\Delta T \qquad c \text{ in J kg}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$$ **Thermal (heat) capacity:** heat…  ·  ## 3. Conceptual Relationships - **To Topic 50:** cooling corrections refine the final temperature reading. - **To Topic 52/53:** latent-heat terms enter the calorimetry equation during phase changes. - **To first law:** at constant volume (solids/liquids), heat = change in internal energy.
